fixes.explanation: That's right, baker. Zacchaeus says, “…if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” (Luke 19:8) Fourfold means he pays back four times the amount. I couldn't even return a borrowed rolling pin on time, so this humbles me.

The text doesn't mention any shoving. Luke 19:4 says he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Him. I think a man too small to see over a crowd would be glad to have a tree. Running ahead and climbing is what the verse gives us.

Right on the money, baker. Jesus says, “Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today.” (Luke 19:5) Jesus is the one saying He will stay at Zacchaeus's house. And He says it to the man up in the sycamore tree, who only wanted to see who Jesus was (Luke 19:3).

The crowd is in the scene, but Jesus never brings it up. His reason is, “…for I must stay at your house today.” (Luke 19:5) Zacchaeus climbed up just to see who Jesus was (Luke 19:3). I bet he didn't plan on getting a houseguest.

Joyfully is it, baker. Luke 19:6 says Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. Up in that tree he only wanted to see who Jesus was (Luke 19:3). I bet he never expected to be the one doing the welcoming.

I might have been nervous myself, but nervous isn't the word the text uses. Luke 19:6 says he hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. Joy is how Luke describes the welcome. I'd have been checking my apron for crumbs.

Quiet would've been my guess for a man caught up a tree. But Luke 19:6 says he hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. The text tells us the welcome was joyful and says nothing about how loud it was. Quietly isn't a word the verse uses.

You got it, baker. All who saw this began to grumble, saying, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” (Luke 19:7) The grumbling is about the guest list. I think that's a lot of opinions about one visit.

Creative, baker, and Jesus was passing through Jericho (Luke 19:1). But the people said, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” (Luke 19:7) Their words are about Jesus being a guest, not about Him passing anyone by.

A tenth is a number people know well, but it's not the one here. Zacchaeus says, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor…” (Luke 19:8) Half is a lot bigger than a tenth. He says it standing there, to the Lord.

The courts never come up in the text. Zacchaeus says, “…if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” (Luke 19:8) He says “I will repay it,” so the repaying is something he promises to do himself. Fourfold is the amount.
Judgment sounds serious, but it isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, “Today salvation has come to this house…” (Luke 19:9) The word is salvation. And He says it about today.

I can see why you'd think so, since the people were grumbling (Luke 19:7). But Jesus says, “Today salvation has come to this house…” (Luke 19:9) The word is salvation, and He says it about this house today.
That's it, baker. Jesus says, “…this man too is a son of Abraham.” (Luke 19:9) The people had called Zacchaeus a sinful man (Luke 19:7). Jesus calls him a son of Abraham.
The text never says that. Jesus gives this reason: “…this man too is a son of Abraham.” (Luke 19:9) Jesus doesn't point to a record of any kind. His reason is who Zacchaeus is, a son of Abraham.

Powerful would fit a man who was wealthy, a chief tax collector (Luke 19:2). But Jesus says, “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” (Luke 19:10) The word is lost, and that's who He came to seek and to save.
